notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0121i.stoa002.opp-l: The parenthetical source references (e.g. 'S. Leo, ep. 31', 'Hadr., col. 19') are the printed edition's indications of the passages from which the forger drew; they are retained as given. Line 1.10: 'in re certa' must be read as 'in re dubia', as in heading III; translated accordingly. Line 1.11: 'cum' read as 'eum', and 'Uti' as 'Licet' or similar. Line 1.12: 'An. in const.' could not be identified with certainty. Line 1.13: 'Qui aliud' read as 'Quid aliud'; 'ad omnem curem' read as 'ad omnem carnem'; the Isaiah quotation follows the text's Latin, which is close to the Vulgate but at points garbled (e.g. 'opera eorum... venio' lacks a verb such as 'scio', supplied in brackets).

Line 4 ends with a corrupt phrase, 'Quod d mus', evidently a mangled form of Romans 5:10 ('quod si, cum inimici essemus...', 'if, while we were enemies...'); it is rendered with [...]. Evident scanning errors are read as follows: 'dareaqt' as clareant; 'domibns' as hominibus (following Wisdom 10:8); 'Voc' as Vae; 'nul' as aut; 'delentione' as detentione; 'honorum' as bonorum ('good men'). 'non olim, sed tunc' is taken as 'not before, but then'. 'diu suis' is odd and may be corrupt; it is rendered as 'his own affairs for a long while'. The clause 'quia ultra provinciae terminos accusandi ante licentia non est, qua audientia rogetur' is obscure, and the rendering is tentative.

Line 3.2: 'quia ille invisibilis' presumably refers to the Father. Line 3.4: 'rectæ Mei' read as 'rectae fidei'; 'non resultavimus' taken as 'non recusavimus/dubitavimus'. Line 3.5: 'liniens' is obscure (perhaps a scanning error) and left untranslated; 'ipse dicilur' read as 'ipse dicitur', referring to the Father. Line 3.6: 'dicitius' read as 'divitias'; 'Eccl.' citations are to Ecclesiasticus (Sirach); the final reference 'Eccl., II' presumably 11. The Gratian reference '24, q. i' is taken as Causa 24, quaestio 1.

nodes.text: The Four Dubious Letters of St Felix I, Pope and Martyr.
Letter 1.
To Bishop Paternus.
On the trials, accusations and defences of [those in] sacred orders.
I. — That detractors and supporters of enemies are to be barred from accusing a bishop.
II. — That the lesser should not be assailed with accusations by the greater.
III. — That in a doubtful matter no definite sentence is to be passed concerning those who have some case against a cleric in the province.
IV. — That clerics are to pursue their actions [in their own province].
V. — How primates ought to conduct themselves towards an accused bishop.
VI. — That judges of the Church should not pronounce sentence in the absence of the one whose case is being heard, and that the slander or voice of a betrayer should not be heard.
To his most dear and beloved fellow bishop Paternus, Felix, bishop, [sends] greeting in the Lord.

The letter of Your Love has made me rejoice greatly (St Leo, Letter 31) and exult in the Lord, for it clearly shows how much you love the catholic faith and how much you detest heretical error. For heresy is exceedingly impious and an enemy of the truth of the Gospel; it seeks not to harm some part, but to tear up the very foundations of the Christian religion. For whomever it seizes for itself it causes to fall not only into this vice but into many other vices; and at the urging of the ancient enemy himself they become persecutors not only of the Church but also of her priests. Let us therefore take care with one mind to correct and pursue such people, and let us strive to free the Church, her faithful and the priests of the Lord from their enemy. Our almighty Redeemer will grant strength to charity and justice (St Gregory, Letter 56, Book 4); he himself will grant us, though placed far from one another, the unity of his Spirit, by whose craftsmanship the Church, like an ark, has been built on the four sides of the world and bound together with a frame of timbers that do not rot and with the pitch of charity, so that it may be disturbed by the hostility of no spirit and by the swell of no wave coming from outside. But just as, under the guidance of his grace, we must ask that no wave coming upon us from outside should throw us into confusion, so we must pray with our whole heart, dearest brother, that the right hand of his providence may drain for us the accumulated bilge-water within. For the devil, our adversary, who rages against the humble, goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour (1 Peter 5); he no longer, as we see, [merely] circles the sheepfolds, but fixes his teeth so firmly in certain necessary members of the Church that no one doubts that, unless the whole provident company of shepherds runs together with one accord, the Lord acting, he will very soon tear apart the whole fold (God forbid).
I. Therefore we bar detractors, who are to be rooted out by divine authority, and supporters of enemies, from accusing a bishop.
II. Likewise, let none of the highest (Hadrian, ch. 19) be assailed by the accusations of the lesser, or perish [by them].
III. Nor [in a doubtful] matter (St Gregory, Letter 30, Book 8) is a definite sentence to be passed, nor is any judgement to be upheld unless it has been held in due order.

IV. If anyone believes that a cleric should be prosecuted on any charges whatever, let him pursue his actions in the province in which (Hadrian, ch. 8) the one prosecuted resides, and let the accuser not suppose that he may be dragged elsewhere or farther away to judgement. But let the one who has been prosecuted, if he holds the judges suspect, be permitted to appeal to the primates.

V. Likewise, let primates examining an accused bishop not pronounce a sentence of condemnation before, relying on apostolic authority, either he confesses himself guilty (An. in const., Book 9, title 40; Theodosian Code; [Causa] 2, q. 3, Irritum esse episcoporum), or he is convicted by innocent witnesses, canonically examined, in accordance with the rules. Otherwise we judge the condemnation of bishops void and unjust, and therefore to be reconsidered by a synod, so that those oppressed may be helped by all in all cases.

VI. Let the judges of the Church beware (Council of Carthage IV, c. 28) of pronouncing sentence in the absence of the one whose case is being heard, for it will be void; and they will also give account in [God's] presence for their action concerning the brethren. But let neither the slander nor the voice of a betrayer be heard. For no one can know a debtor better than he who has endured his injury and (Theodosian Code, const. 3, title 10, Book 10) wickedness. All, therefore, who wish to live devoutly in Christ must suffer reproaches from the impious who are unlike them, and be despised as foolish and mad (Prosper, Sentence 32, from Augustine on Psalm 122), since they lose present goods in order to acquire invisible and future ones. Yet the contempt and mockery of such people will be turned back upon those who harass them; for their abundance will pass into want, and their pride into confusion. And whatever adversity or evil is inflicted on the just is not the punishment of a crime but the testing of virtue. And just as gold becomes better the more it is refined, so the just man, the more he is afflicted (if he bears that affliction patiently), is rendered much purer and dearer to God. Hence the Truth himself says in person (St Matthew 5): Blessed are those who suffer persecution for the sake of justice, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Of such the Lord speaks through Isaiah, saying (Isaiah 66): Hear the word of the Lord, you who tremble at his word. Your brothers, who hate you and cast you out for my name's sake, have said: Let the Lord be glorified, and we shall see [it] in your joy; but they shall be put to shame. A voice of the people from the city, a voice from the temple, the voice of the Lord rendering recompense to his enemies. Before she was in labour, she gave birth; before her delivery came, she bore a male child. Who has ever heard such a thing? And who has seen anything like it? Shall the earth be in labour in one day? Or shall a nation be brought forth at once, because Zion has been in labour and has borne her sons? Shall I, who make others give birth, not myself give birth, says the Lord? Shall I, who grant offspring to others, be barren, says the Lord your God? Rejoice with Jerusalem and exult in her, all you who love her. Rejoice with her with joy, all you who mourn over her, that you may suck and be filled from the breast of her consolation, that you may milk and abound in delights from her glory of every kind; for thus says the Lord: Behold, I will turn upon her like a river of peace, and like an overflowing torrent the glory of the nations, which you shall suck. You shall be carried at the breasts, and they will fondle you upon the knees. As a mother fondles someone, so will I comfort you, and in Jerusalem you shall be comforted. You shall see, and your heart shall rejoice, and your bones shall sprout like grass. And the hand of the Lord shall be known to his servants, and he shall be indignant with his enemies. For behold, the Lord will come in fire, and his chariot like a whirlwind, to render his fury in indignation, and his rebuke in a flame of fire. For in fire the Lord will judge, and with his sword [he will judge] all flesh, and those slain by the Lord shall be many. Those who sanctified themselves and thought themselves clean in the gardens behind the door within, who ate the flesh of swine, and the abomination, and the mouse, shall be consumed together, says the Lord. But I [know] their works and their thoughts; I am coming to gather [them] with all nations and tongues; and they shall come and see my glory, and I will set a sign among them. And I will send those of them who have been saved to the nations, to the sea, to Africa, to Lydia, those who draw the bow, to Italy and Greece, to the islands far away, to those who have not heard of me and have not seen my glory. And they shall proclaim my glory to the nations, and they shall bring all your brothers out of all the nations as a gift to the Lord, on horses and in chariots and in litters and on mules and in carriages, to my holy mountain Jerusalem, says the Lord, just as if the children of Israel were to bring an offering in a clean vessel into the house of the Lord. And I will take some of them for priests and Levites, says the Lord. For as the new heavens and the new earth, which I make to stand before me, says the Lord, so shall your seed and your name stand. And there shall be month after month, and sabbath after sabbath, and all flesh shall come to worship before my face, says the Lord. And they shall go out and see the corpses of the men who have transgressed against me. Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched, and they shall be a sight to all flesh until they are sated with seeing. What else do detractors do (St Gregory, Letter 45, Book 8) but blow into the dust and stir up earth into their own eyes? And the more they blow out detraction, the less of the truth they see? Yet such people, dearest brother, are to be borne with and corrected, because they are blind and leaders of the blind (St Matthew 15). With these things, dearest one, I have briefly answered your enquiries, which we command you and all bishops to hold according to the rules. Yet we admonish your prudence, brother, to strive to labour with all your strength for the state of the Church and her priests, to keep the order of the holy Roman and apostolic Church in all things, and not to permit the decrees of the saints to be violated, but to instruct all whom you can, so that you may present fruitful sheaves to the Lord. Farewell. Given on the Nones of June, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Claudius and Aurelian.
LETTER II.
ON THE AUTHORITY OF THE JUDGE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE, AND ON ACCUSED BISHOPS.
Felix, bishop, to all the bishops established throughout the provinces of Gaul, greeting in the Lord.

It is not in doubt that God is the author of good works and spiritual pursuits (St Leo, Letter 32), who stirs the minds of [those who undertake] them and helps their actions. Hence your letters, springing from the good zeal and the integrity of faith of your devotion, made me rejoice; but because of your affliction and contrition they saddened [me] in great part. For sad, I read your sad letters (Peter Chrysologus, letter to Eutyches), and I ran through the mournful writing with due grief: for just as the peace of the Churches, the concord of her priests and the tranquillity of the people give us joy to hear, so the affliction of our brothers afflicts and casts us down. Yet do not be greatly saddened (St Gregory, Letter 45, Book 8), because, as the Truth itself says in person: If you were of this world, the world would love what was its own; but because you are not of this world, but I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hates you (St John 15), that is, the lovers of the world. Yet whatever these people say or do against you, always keep your faith whole and have a pure conscience, so that your spirit and soul may be kept whole on the day of the Lord (1 Thessalonians 5). For our part, to support you, we have called more than seventy of our brothers and fellow bishops, with whom we have decreed that the matters set out below are to be dealt with according to the rules. For when your letters had been read through in the hearing of all, which (as you know) contained many complaints of your oppressions, and the decrees concerning the accusations of bishops [had been read], the holy synod said: These are the things which from now on, because of the plots of wicked men who rage indiscriminately against the Church and against churchmen, we also wish to be kept most firmly in the world: If any bishop is accused by such accusers as are to be admitted, after he has been approached by them in charity so that he may amend the matter itself, and he has refused to correct it, then, not before, let his case be brought canonically to the highest primates, who must convene a council according to the rules in a fitting place within that province, at a fitting time, that is, in autumn or summer, so that he may be heard there by all the bishops of that province. And he himself, having been summoned according to the rules, must be present there, unless illness (Theodosian Code, Book 9, title 1, const. 10; [Causa] 3, q. 2, Si episcopus suis fuerit) or some other grave necessity detains him: for there is no licence to accuse beyond the bounds of the province before a hearing is sought there. For if he has been despoiled of his own goods or those of the Church entrusted to him, or (which God forbid, and which ought to be foreign to all the faithful) has been ejected from his own see, or has been separated from his sheep by some detention, then, canonically, before he is restored to his former state with every privilege of his office, and all his goods that had been taken from him through the plots of his enemies are restored according to the laws, he cannot be summoned or judged, unless he himself, for his own need (yet not to be judged in the least), chooses to come of his own accord. In no way, therefore, is he to be asked by anyone to answer before everything that he had lost through the instigations of his enemies is restored most completely to his control by the honourable council in lawful order, and the prelate is returned with all honour to his former state; and when he himself has freely and securely arranged and put in order his own affairs for a long while, then according to the rules, within four or five or seven months, as he finds it possible, and not before, having been summoned in time, let him come to the case in a lawful and canonical council, and, if it then seems just, let him answer the charges of his accusers. For this must be provided for above all, that he is not forced to answer before these things are done, because contention is always to be avoided. For to take the bishopric from a bishop (Council of Africa, c. 87) before the outcome of his case appears can seem lawful to no Christian, because such presumption is sacrilege, and the author of such things is sacrilegious. But if the bishop is ill ([Causa] 3, q. 3, Si aegrotans), or some grave necessity detains him, let him send a representative to the synod on his behalf. Nor is the one against whom a charge is brought to be suspended from communion (Third Council of Carthage, can. 7), unless, having been summoned by letter to plead his case on the day appointed by the chosen judges, he fails to appear: that is, unless some necessity has prevented him within the space of the months mentioned, and more besides, as the case requires. But if both parties come to plead the case, since one should not be heard without the other, it must be enquired at the trial of what manner of life, faith and suspicion the accusers are, or with what intention they do this: for none should be admitted to this except men of good life and right faith, namely those who are free of all suspicion, are distinguished by a good life, and are not infamous. But if the persons of the accusers appear culpable at the trial ([Causa] 3, q. 10, Si accusatorum personae) of bishops (the same, Council of Carthage), let them not be admitted to make the charge, unless they wish to plead their own cases (yet not criminal ones) or the Church's. For an infamous person ([Causa] 3, q. 7, Infamis persona) can be neither a procurator nor a representative. And in the absence of the opponent ([Causa] 3, q. 9, Absente adversario) let the accuser not be heard; nor will a sentence pronounced by a judge in the absence of the other party have any validity (see Anianus on the Sentences of Paul, Book 5, titles 2 and 5); nor can an absent person be accused through another ([Causa] 3, q. 9, Absens per alium), or accuse, nor let a relative of theirs be admitted. No one, therefore, should be produced from province to province (see the third Novel of Book 3, and Anianus, and the Theodosian Code, const. 4, Book 2, title 1), or to the court, except on the report of the judge to whom appeal has been made, that is, so that the plaintiff always follows the court of the defendant. But if anyone feels the judge is against him, let him raise the cry of appeal, which ought to be denied to no one (up to here chapter 5 of Hadrian's collection, with some things inserted here and there). Foreign judgements ([Causa] 3, q. 6, Peregrina judicia) we forbid by a general sanction, because it is unworthy that one be judged by outsiders who ought to have judges from his own province (Hadrian's collection, from the Theodosian Code, const. 10, title 1, Book 9) and chosen by himself. These things, brothers, have been decreed unanimously in synod for the help and defence of you and of all our fellow bishops, so that if perhaps some fools (Second Council of Spain, c. 15), deceived by the error of diabolical deception, wish to accuse you, they may come to their senses when they read or hear these things and return to the concord of unity; and what was before [deserving] of punishment will pass into glory. For without doubt there are many who (in the apostle's words), with itching ears, turn their hearing away from the truth and are turned to fables (1 Timothy 4), and go over to doing harm to good men. And the same apostle (the same council cited) says of the ignorance of unbelievers: If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2). Likewise, if these men had perfectly known and loved the Lord, they would never have troubled his servants, nor persecuted them by words or deeds. If [...], we have been reconciled to God through the death of his Son (Romans 5), why do we pursue our brothers? Why do we trouble the state of the Church of God, and afflict those who ought to serve her? For the martyrs suffered (the same council cited), yet their souls were not slain in the suffering of the body, as the mouth of Truth testifies: Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul (Matthew 10). Here it must be recognised that, if the souls of the martyrs cannot be extinguished by torments when the body has been destroyed, neither ought the souls of preachers and teachers to have been persecuted or troubled and turned away from the service of God, since they do not perish with their bodies. Such troublers of the Church not only do the evils mentioned, but also curse the shrines of the martyrs (Council of Gangra, ch. 20, in Dionysius' version). Therefore we have decreed in the aforesaid synod, and we command you and all the Churches to keep and do it, that masses be celebrated over the shrines of the martyrs, so that their memorials cannot be destroyed by such people nor their veneration forbidden. But you, brothers, do not be greatly troubled, do not be vexed, but be strengthened in the Lord and in the might of his glory (Ephesians 6). Meanwhile hold these things, decreed by apostolic authority, as your support; and know that we are always ready, even (if need be) unto death, to accomplish whatever may be necessary for you (with the Lord's help). They, however, by God's doing, will perish, and you will stand, provided that your labour is not in vain but full of faith and charity. Woe, says the prophet, to him who gives drink to his friend, mixing in his gall (Habakkuk 2). And again the most wise Solomon says (these same words in the letter of Felix II to the Egyptians): He who speaks wicked things cannot be hidden, nor will the judgement that rebukes pass him by. For in the thoughts of the ungodly there will be an inquiry, and the hearing of his words will come to the Lord, to the rebuke of his iniquities. For the ear of jealousy hears all things, and the tumult of murmurings will not be hidden (Wisdom 1). If they had been willing to embrace these things with their own sound sense, they would not have slipped into a reprobate sense; but, guarding their words carefully through the fear of God, they would surely have kept the godly definition of the holy fathers without any presumption to do harm. For the sacred word says: Good counsel will preserve you, and a good mind will guard you (Proverbs 2). For such accusations and detractions do not proceed spiritually from the saving springs towards the gaining of eternal life, and therefore the blessed apostle Paul, forewarning us fittingly, says: One should not be wiser than it is fitting to be wise, but be wise unto sobriety (Romans 12), persevering in the definition of godliness. For those who pass over these things are not only harmed, falling from their own firmness, but have left to men a memorial of their folly, so that in the things in which they sinned they could not be hidden. For glory and disgrace are in speech (Ecclesiasticus 5), and in the speech of a man's tongue is his fall. And therefore it is fitting that this demonstration of their faults be inserted in our acts, so that you may no longer suffer such things while they sow tares and scandals, but may deserve to rejoice in your offices and teachings. Let them therefore blush, and hasten to withdraw such and similar blasphemy, if they do not wish to be separated from our priestly college and torn away from the fellowship of the whole Christian people. For although we could have said and written much more, and very necessary, on these matters, which is found established in the decrees of the apostolic see and by the apostles and their successors, namely our predecessors, yet it seemed better to us to close the letter with a prayer. May almighty God and his only-begotten Son, our Saviour Christ, grant you this incentive: that you help with all your strength all our brothers and fellow bishops who labour under any tribulations, and, suffering with them, carry the cross of the same Lord and Saviour, so that you may appear before all as his true disciples, and so that both you and those who are with you may possess, here and in the future, the better things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him (1 Corinthians 2). Through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to almighty God for ever and ever. Amen. I wish you well, dearest brothers. Given on the fifth day before the Ides of August, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Claudius and Paternus (year of Christ 269, Dionysius not yet dead).
LETTER III.
TO BISHOP BENIGNUS.
I. Those err who maintain that the Son does not see the Father, on the ground that no one has ever seen God.
II. Those err who affirm that the Son is less than the Father, because He is invisible, but the Son visible.
To his most beloved brother Bishop Benignus, Felix, bishop, greeting in the Lord.

Receiving the letters of your fraternity (Zacharias, letter 5), in which you questioned me about teachings of the faith which were held by others otherwise than the mysteries of the right faith contain, we have not refused, as the Lord has granted, to reply out of love for [your] fraternity. For doubtful and greater matters have always been accustomed to receive their settlement from this holy see, from the time of the apostles, who furnished it with their teachings. And therefore you have done rightly in wishing that you and the others be strengthened and instructed by the counsels of this holy see.

I. — For your letter, and that of your brothers, contained [the report] that certain people say that the Son cannot properly see the Father, because it is written: For no one has ever seen God. And others invent [this]: The Son is less than the Father for this reason, that the Father bears witness to him. And some chatter that He is less than the Father for this reason, that He [the Father] is called invisible (John 1; Matthew 17; Mark 9; Luke 9; 1 Corinthians 9; Colossians 1; 1 Timothy 1), while the Son is shown to be visible. For these men, ignorant of the laws of the divine Scriptures and of the apostles, fabricate such things out of their own or a counterfeit understanding, and seek to lead astray the hearts of the faithful (1). But let us return to the origin of the very spring, from which we teach, by the clearer testimonies of the Old and New Testament, that the Son always could and can see the Father, as Solomon says: With you is wisdom, which knows your works, which was present with you when you made the world, and it knows what is pleasing in your eyes. And the Lord in the Gospel: No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal [him]. And again: No one has ever seen God except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father; he has made [him] known. And again he said to the Jews: You do not know him, but I know him. And if I say that I do not know him, I shall be like you, a liar. Likewise there: He who is from God, he knows him. And again: I know him, because I am from him. See, we have shown that the Son always sees the Father. How do they assert that he cannot see the Father, in whose bosom he is known to abide? If you go through the divine Scriptures with a clear mind, you will find not only the Father bearing witness to the Son, but the whole inseparable Trinity together, as the Lord himself declares, who says: I am the one who bears witness about myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness about me (John 8). And again: If I bear witness about myself, my testimony is true, because I know where I come from and where I am going (ibid.). And of the Holy Spirit: When the Paraclete comes, the Spirit of truth, he will bear witness about me (John 15). Consider, I beg, consider that among those in whom one power of testifying is shown, none is judged either greater or lesser than another.

II. — We have already said this quite often: that according to the form of man the Son is called visible, but according to the substance of the Godhead he is proclaimed invisible, as the apostle Paul attests: O the depth, he says, of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgements, and unsearchable his ways (Romans 11)! And in Isaiah: To whom do you reckon him like, since he himself is invisible (Isaiah 40)? And again the Apostle: To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given among the Gentiles, to preach the unsearchable riches of Christ, and to enlighten all [as to] what is the dispensation of the mystery hidden from the ages, in which he created all things (Ephesians 3). Likewise he himself: Who is, he says, the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1). And to the Colossians: I Paul, a minister, who now rejoice in my sufferings for you, and fill up in my flesh what is lacking of the tribulations of Christ for his body, which is the Church, of which I was made a minister according to the dispensation of God for the ministry of Christ, which was hidden from the ages and from the generations (ibid.). Likewise there: That their hearts may be comforted in charity, unto all the riches of the fullness of understanding, unto the knowledge of the mystery, which is Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2). And in Psalm 76: Your way is in the sea, and your paths in many waters, and your footsteps will not be known. And in Solomon: The wisdom of God, which precedes all things, who will search out (Ecclesiasticus 1)? Likewise there: To whom has the root of wisdom been revealed? And who has known her subtleties (ibid.)? Likewise there: To whom has the discipline of wisdom been made manifest, and who has understood the multiplicity of her approach (ibid.)? Likewise there: For the works of the Lord alone are wonderful, and glorious and hidden, and his works are unseen by men (Ecclesiasticus 11). See, as the Father is invisible, so too we find the Son [to be]. How then is he judged inferior to the Father by those who say what you have reported, in that he deigned to be seen by us in the flesh? Do not believe such men, and teach others to turn away from their opinion. Serve the Lord, then, in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling (Psalm 2). Lay hold of discipline, lest you perish from the just way. This indeed (Causa 24, q. 1, "A recta ergo fide") is the living tradition of the apostles, this the true charity, which is to be preached, and truly loved and cherished, and held faithfully by all. This is the holy and apostolic mother of all churches (Agatho, letter to the Emperor Constantine, act 4 of the Sixth Ecumenical Council), the Church of Christ, which through the grace of almighty God is proved never to have strayed from the path of apostolic tradition, nor has it succumbed to being corrupted by heretical novelties, but as at the beginning it received the rule of the Christian faith from its founders, the princes of the apostles of Christ, it remains unblemished to the end, according to the divine promise of the Lord and Saviour himself, who said to the prince of his disciples in his Gospels: Peter, he said, behold, Satan has demanded to sift you as one who sifts wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brothers (Luke 22). Let your excellent prudence therefore consider how good it is to persist in the stewardship entrusted to you, and in the right faith, and to resist heretics and the rivals of Christ, and never to turn aside from the path of truth. For the Lord and Saviour of all, whose faith it is, who did not hesitate to die for us and redeemed us with his own blood, promised that the faith of blessed Peter would not fail, and admonished him to strengthen his brothers: and that the apostolic pontiffs, the predecessors of my littleness, have confidently done this has always been known to all. And my smallness, though unequal and least, nevertheless desires to be their follower, on account of the ministry undertaken by divine favour. For woe to us who have taken up the burden of this ministry, if we neglect to preach the truth of our Saviour Jesus Christ which the apostles preached. Woe to us if we suppress by silence the truth which we are commanded to pay out to the money-changers, that is, to instruct and teach the Christian peoples. What shall we say at the future judgement of Christ himself, if we are ashamed to preach the truth of his words? What will become of us when Christ our God, the just judge, demands a strict account of the souls entrusted to us and of the office undertaken (1 Corinthians 9; Matthew 25)? Therefore, brothers, I exhort your love (St Leo, letter against the Manichaeans), I implore and warn you to keep watch with what care you can and ought, to search out heretics and enemies of the holy Church of God, and to root them out from sound minds as far as you are able, with what severity you can, lest this plague spread more widely. For just as he who has more diligently carried out what benefits the salvation of the people entrusted to him will have from God the reward of a worthy recompense, so whoever has been unwilling to guard his people against the authors of sacrilegious persuasion will not be able to excuse himself before the tribunal of the Lord from the guilt of negligence. Given on the Nones of February, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Claudius and Paternus (269, Felix not yet elected).
LETTER IV (1).
TO BISHOP MAXIMUS AND THE CLERGY OF ALEXANDRIA.
A fragment on the divinity and humanity of Christ.

Concerning the incarnation of the Word and the faith, we believe in our Lord Jesus Christ born of the Virgin Mary, because he is the eternal Son of God: for the Son of God did not assume a man so that there should be another besides himself; but, existing as perfect God, he was at the same time made perfect man, incarnate of the Virgin.
